Its specification `Combinatorics.Selection.NSelection.mem_selectFirstNBy_iff` says that $p$ is selected exactly when $p\in s$ and its key is among the first $N$ keys; `Combinatorics.Selection.NSelection.selectFirstNBy_subset` gives inclusion in $s$.

Source header “The leftmost selection mechanism”; Public declarations: - `Combinatorics.Selection.NSelection.rank_lt_card_of_mem` and `Combinatorics.Selection.NSelection.rank_lt_rank_of_lt` show that $p\in s$ gives $\operatorname{rank}(s,p)<|s|$, and that $p\in s$ and $p<q$ give $\operatorname{rank}(s,p)<\operatorname{rank}(s,q)$. `Combinatorics.Selection.NSelection.rank_injOn` states injectivity on $s$; `Combinatorics.Selection.NSelection.image_rank_eq_range` states $\operatorname{rank}(s) '' s=\operatorname{Finset.range}(|s|)$. - `Combinatorics.Selection.NSelection.card_selectFirstN` gives $|\operatorname{selectFirstN}(N,s)|=\min(N,|s|)$. `Combinatorics.Selection.NSelection.selectFirstN_image_orderIso` states that for an order isomorphism $e:\alpha\simeq_o\beta$, $(\operatorname{selectFirstN}(N,s)).\operatorname{image}(e)= \operatorname{selectFirstN}(N,s.\operatorname{image}(e))$. `Combinatorics.Selection.NSelection.card_filter_selectFirstN_of_downwardClosed` gives $|\operatorname{selectFirstN}(N,s)\cap P|=\min(N,|s\cap P|)$ when $P$ is downward closed on $s$. `Combinatorics.Selection.NSelection.rank_eq_zero_iff_isLeast` characterizes least candidates by rank zero.

Source header “The rightmost selection mechanism is the order dual of the leftmost one”; Public declarations: The declarations in `Combinatorics.Selection.NSelection` derive rightmost facts by transporting finite sets through `OrderDual`: - `Combinatorics.Selection.NSelection.toDual_mem_image_toDual_iff` preserves membership under `toDual`. `Combinatorics.Selection.NSelection.rank_image_toDual` gives $\operatorname{rank}(s.image(\operatorname{toDual}),\operatorname{toDual}(q)) =|\{p\in s:q<p\}|$. `Combinatorics.Selection.NSelection.reverseRank_image_toDual` gives $|\{p\in s.image(\operatorname{toDual}):\operatorname{toDual}(q)<p\}| =|\{p\in s:p<q\}|$. - `Combinatorics.Selection.NSelection.mem_selectFirstN_image_toDual_iff` and `Combinatorics.Selection.NSelection.mem_selectLastN_image_toDual_iff` state, respectively, $\operatorname{toDual}(q)\in\operatorname{selectFirstN}(N,s.image(\operatorname{toDual})) \iff q\in\operatorname{selectLastN}(N,s)$ and $\operatorname{toDual}(q)\in\operatorname{selectLastN}(N,s.image(\operatorname{toDual})) \iff q\in\operatorname{selectFirstN}(N,s)$. `Combinatorics.Selection.NSelection.selectFirstN_image_toDual` and `Combinatorics.Selection.NSelection.image_toDual_selectFirstN` state, respectively, $\operatorname{selectFirstN}(N,s.image(\operatorname{toDual}))= \operatorname{selectLastN}(N,s).image(\operatorname{toDual})$ and $\operatorname{selectFirstN}(N,s).image(\operatorname{toDual})= \operatorname{selectLastN}(N,s.image(\operatorname{toDual}))$; and `Combinatorics.Selection.NSelection.selectLastN_eq_image_selectFirstN` states $\operatorname{selectLastN}(N,s)= \operatorname{selectFirstN}(N,s.image(\operatorname{toDual})).image(\operatorname{ofDual})$.

Source header “Lower-tail comparison for first-N selection”; Public declarations: The source and candidate populations may use different label types. The source positions are compared by value thresholds, while the candidate labels are selected by their own linear order. A monotonicity hypothesis connects that order to the candidate positions. The resulting count comparison is a finite selector theorem and does not depend on a branching-walk or cloud representation. - `filter_card_le_filter_selectFirstN` proves that if `retained ⊆ source`, `retained.card ≤ N`, `(source.filter (fun p => position p ≤ a)).card ≤ (rightCandidates.filter (fun q => candidatePosition q ≤ a)).card` for every `a`, and `q ≤ p → candidatePosition q ≤ candidatePosition p` on `rightCandidates`, then `(retained.filter (fun p => position p ≤ a)).card ≤ ((selectFirstN N rightCandidates).filter (fun q => candidatePosition q ≤ a)).card` for every `a`. - `exists_selectFirstN_le_of_mem` gives a one particle consequence: for `N > 0` and `p ∈ source`, there exists `q ∈ selectFirstN N rightCandidates` with `candidatePosition q ≤ position p` under the same threshold and monotonicity hypotheses.

Source header “Selecting the first N points of a possibly infinite population”; Public declarations: Write $K(p)=\operatorname{valueKey}(value,p)$ for the selected-order key. Unless otherwise stated, these definitions and results assume linear orders on particle labels and observed values. - `Combinatorics.Selection.NSelection.IsLowerFiniteBy`: every candidate has finitely many candidates with key at most its own, $\forall p\in C,\;\{q\in C:K(q)\le K(p)\}$ is finite. - `Combinatorics.Selection.NSelection.lowerSection` is the pointwise set $\{q\in C(\omega):K_\omega(q)\le K_\omega(p)\}$, and `lowerFiniteDomain` is the set of samples where `IsLowerFiniteBy` holds.

Source header “Totalized first-N selection”; Public declarations: - `Combinatorics.Selection.NSelection.selectFirstNFromSetTotalized`: the canonical first-`N` finite set on the lower-finite domain, and `∅` outside that domain. - `Combinatorics.Selection.NSelection.selectFirstNFromSetTotalized_spec`: on the lower-finite domain, the totalized selector satisfies `IsFirstNBy N`.

It concludes `lower * ∑ finish, (kernel ^ n) start finish ≤ eigenvalue ^ n * weight start ≤ upper * ∑ finish, (kernel ^ n) start finish`. The root-indexed construction rootedCapStoppedPopulation maps each retained local address below an observable root address; rootedCapStoppedPopulation_succ_subset shows that each next-generation address is a selected child of a retained address. Let \(C_{m,n}\) denote the expected ordered pair contribution whose most recent common ancestor is at generation \(m\), with \(n+1\) generations below it. Put \(M_\varphi=\int\texttt{crossPotentialWeight }\varphi\,(-1)\,\xi\,d\mu(\xi)\) and \(P_{\mathrm{sp}}=\texttt{tiltedIncrementFieldLaw }\varphi\,\mu\), and \(E_m=\{z\mid\texttt{history }m\,x\,z\in \texttt{affineCorridorPrefix }m\,a\,v\,\Delta\}\). Summing this estimate over the possible ancestor generations gives \[ \sum_{m=0}^{N-1}C_{m,N-m-1} \le \sum_{m=0}^{N-1}e^{-2x}e^{2u}q_{N-m-1}^{2} M_\varphi e^{x-a-vm} P_{\mathrm{sp}}(E_m). \] The one-use affine-corridor continuation estimate supplying the bound is in `MRCA/Lemmas/AffineCorridorContinuation.lean`.

Source header “Survival of finite partial steps”; Public declarations: - `partialStepSurvivalWeight` is the recursive total weight of surviving histories; `partialStepHistoryWeight` is its explicit sum over finite noise vectors. - `partialStepSurvivalWeight_zero`, `partialStepSurvivalWeight_succ`, `partialStepHistoryWeight_succ`, and `partialStepHistoryWeight_eq_survivalWeight` give the initial value, one-step recursion, and equality of the two descriptions.

Source header “Iteration of partial random steps”; Public declarations: - `survivalProbability` is the probability under the finite product law $\nu^n$ that the partial-step path survives for $n$ transitions. - `survivalProbability_succ` gives the one-step integral recursion for $Q_n(a)=\mathbb P(\text{the step path survives $n$ transitions from }a)$.

Source header “Paths of partial random steps”; Public declarations: - `runPartialSteps` consumes a finite noise history and returns `none` at the first killed step or `some` of the terminal state. - `Survives` and `EndsIn` define the finite-history survival and target events; `SurvivesPrefix` and `EndsInPrefix` are their first-$n$-coordinate versions on an infinite noise sequence.

Source header “Sub-Markov kernels”; Public declarations: - `IsSubMarkovKernel` means `κ a univ ≤ 1` for every source state; its `measure_le_one` theorem bounds every measurable target mass by one. - `IsSubMarkovKernel.isFiniteKernel`, `isSubMarkovKernel_zero`, and `IsMarkovKernel.isSubMarkovKernel` provide finiteness, the zero-kernel instance, and the inclusion of Markov kernels.

Source header “Remaining mass of iterated kernels”; Public declarations: - `remainingMass` defines $M_n(x)=(K^n)(x,S)$; `remainingMass_zero` and `remainingMass_add` give $M_0(x)=1$ and $M_{m+n}(x)=\int M_n(y)\,(K^m)(x,dy)$. - `mul_pow_apply_le_pow_add_apply_of_mem` and `mul_pow_apply_le_remainingMass_add_of_mem` give the two-block lower bound $c(K^m)(x,E)\le(K^{m+n})(x,B)$ when the second-block mass is at least $c$ on the measurable entrance set $E$; the latter takes $B=S$. `mul_remainingMass_le_remainingMass_add` is the uniform-survival case.

Source header “Blocking bounds for remaining kernel mass”; Public declarations: For a sub-Markov kernel $K$ with remaining mass $M_n(x)=(K^n)(x,S)$: - If every $b$-step block has mass at least $p$ uniformly in its starting state and $b>0$, `pow_succ_div_le_remainingMass` gives $p^{\lfloor n/b\rfloor+1}\le M_n(x)$. - If every $b$-step block has mass at most $u$, `remainingMass_le_pow_div` gives $M_n(x)\le u^{\lfloor n/b\rfloor}$.

Source header “Kernels returning to a measurable subset”; Public declarations: - `returnKernel` is the $n$-step kernel restricted to the measurable set $A$ at both endpoints; `returnKernel_apply` and `returnKernel_apply_univ` identify its values with the corresponding ambient transition masses. `returnKernel.instIsSubMarkovKernel` preserves sub-Markovness. - `mul_le_returnKernel_apply_univ_of_entrance` combines a uniform entrance bound into a measurable core with a uniform transition from that core back to $A$, yielding a lower bound for one return block.

Source header “Finite return sequences with a final bridge”; Public declarations: - `returnKernelSequenceExit` composes a finite sequence of returns to `core` with a final bridge to `target`. If every return block has mass at least `p` on `core`, and the exit block has mass at least `q` from every core state, then `mul_pow_le_returnKernelSequenceExit_apply_univ` gives the lower bound `p ^ lengths.length * q` for the composed kernel. - For a sub-Markov kernel, `returnKernelSequenceExit_apply_univ_le` bounds the mass of this constrained sequence by the unrestricted transition mass `(K ^ (returnKernelSequenceLength lengths + exitLength))(x, target)`.

Source header “Finite sequences of return blocks”; Public declarations: - `returnKernelSequence` composes the return kernels for the finite list of block lengths, in list order; `returnKernelSequenceLength` is their sum, as stated by `returnKernelSequenceLength_eq_sum`. - If every listed block has mass at least $p$ from every state in $A$, `pow_le_returnKernelSequence_apply_univ` gives total mass at least $p^{\operatorname{length}(lengths)}$.

Source header “Iterating positive test-function bounds for kernels”; Public declarations: - If $f:S\to[0,\infty]$ is measurable and $\lambda f(x)\le\int f(y)K(x,dy)$ for every $x$, then `pow_lintegral_lower_bound_of_subEigenfunction` gives $\lambda^n f(x)\le\int f(y)(K^n)(x,dy)$ for every $n$. - For a sub-Markov kernel, if additionally $f\le1$, `pow_mul_le_remainingMass_of_subEigenfunction` gives $\lambda^n f(x)\le M_n(x)$.

Source header “Asymptotic logarithmic rates for probability sequences”; Public declarations: * `ProbabilityTheory.eventually_probabilityRate_ge_finiteProductRate`: for an ENNReal-valued probability sequence $p_n\le1$, if $r_nm_i(n)\to c_i$ and $\prod_i \exp(a_i m_i(n))\le p_n$ eventually, then for every $\varepsilon>0$ eventually $p_n>0$ and $\sum_i c_i a_i-\varepsilon\le r_n\log p_n$. * `ProbabilityTheory.limsup_probabilityRate_le_of_eventually_le_pow`: if $p_n\le q^{m_n}$ eventually, $r_n\ge0$ eventually, $r_nm_n\to c$, $p_n>0$ eventually, and $r_n\log p_n$ is lower-cobounded, then \[ \limsup_{n\to\infty} r_n\log p_n\le c\log q. \]

Source header “Almost-sure finiteness of the first Brownian unit window”; Public declarations: The public theorem in this file is: - `ProbabilityTheory.IsBrownianReal.measure_firstNonnegativeWindowStart_ne_top_eq_one`: for a Brownian path $B$, the first time $T$ with $B(T+u)\ge B(T)$ for every $u\in[0,1]$ is finite almost surely. - `ProbabilityTheory.IsBrownianReal.tendsto_measure_firstNonnegativeWindowStartUpTo_ne_top`: the probability that $T^{n+1}<\infty$ tends to one.

Source header “Continuity of the first Brownian unit-window time”; Public declarations: The public theorem in this file is: - `ProbabilityTheory.IsBrownianReal.ae_continuousAt_firstNonnegativeWindowStart`: the map $f\mapsto T(f)$ is continuous at almost every Brownian path. - `ProbabilityTheory.IsBrownianReal.ae_continuousAt_firstNonnegativeWindowStartUpTo_of_one_lt`: for $1<s<\infty$, the map $f\mapsto T^s(f)$ is continuous at almost every Brownian path.

Source header “Endpoint returns and descending Brownian hitting times”; Public declarations: The public theorem in this file is: - `ProbabilityTheory.IsBrownianReal.ae_endpointReturn_hittingTimeRightLimit`: almost surely, if the first qualifying unit window starts at $t$ and returns to its starting level $-x$ at $t+1$, then $\tau_x=t$, $t+1<\tau_y$ for every $y>x$, and for every $v>t+1$ there is $y>x$ with $\tau_y\le v$. This is the pathwise identification of the unit-length jump used in equation (2.2) of Lemma 2.3 in Erwin Bolthausen, *On a Functional Central Limit Theorem for Random Walks Conditioned to Stay Positive*, Ann. Probab. 4(3) (1976), 480--485, DOI 10.1214/aop/1176996098. The separate probabilistic assertion that the hitting-time process has no jump of this length comes from the Lévy decomposition cited there.

Source header “The finite-horizon first-window boundary event”; Internal proof declarations: The proof-support lemma in this file is: - `ProbabilityTheory.IsBrownianReal.measure_firstNonnegativeWindowStartUpTo_eq_last`: for $s>1$, the probability that $T^s=s-1$ is zero. This is the fixed-time non-atom step in equation (2.3) of Lemma 2.3 in Erwin Bolthausen, *On a Functional Central Limit Theorem for Random Walks Conditioned to Stay Positive*, Ann. Probab. 4(3) (1976), 480--485, DOI 10.1214/aop/1176996098.

Source header “Endpoint return of the first Brownian unit window”; Internal proof declarations: The supporting lemmas in this file are: - `ProbabilityTheory.IsBrownianReal.measure_firstNonnegativeWindowStart_endpointReturn_eq_zero`: the same assertion for the unrestricted first window. These are equation (2.2) of Lemma 2.3 in Erwin Bolthausen, *On a Functional Central Limit Theorem for Random Walks Conditioned to Stay Positive*, Ann. Probab. 4(3) (1976), 480--485, DOI 10.1214/aop/1176996098. Bolthausen cites the Lévy decomposition of descending hitting times to exclude a fixed excursion length. This proof conditions at a rational time inside the excursion and uses the atomless first-passage law.

Source header “Brownian paths increase somewhere on every time interval”; Internal proof declarations: The supporting lemmas in this file are: - `ProbabilityTheory.IsBrownianReal.ae_exists_positiveWindowBeforeUnit`: almost every Brownian path has a positive-duration window inside $[0,1]$ on which it stays above its value at the window's start. The proof uses independent increments on equal subdivisions and the fact that every nondegenerate centered Gaussian increment has a fixed positive probability of being positive. This is the probabilistic step in Erwin Bolthausen, *On a Functional Central Limit Theorem for Random Walks Conditioned to Stay Positive*, Lemma 2.2, p. 481, Ann. Probab. 4(3) (1976), 480--485, DOI 10.1214/aop/1176996098.

Source header “Interior returns of the first Brownian unit window”; Internal proof declarations: The supporting lemmas in this file are: - `ProbabilityTheory.IsBrownianReal.measure_tripleRunningMinimumContact_eq_zero`: Bolthausen's three-contact event $U$ has probability zero. - `ProbabilityTheory.IsBrownianReal.measure_pastMinimumGap_eq_futureMinimum`: the equality event between the past minimum gap and the future running minimum has probability zero.

Source header “Almost-sure continuity of Brownian first-window shifts”; Public declarations: The public theorems in this file are: - `ProbabilityTheory.IsBrownianReal.ae_continuousAt_shiftAtFirstNonnegativeWindowStart`: $f\mapsto\Phi(f)$ is continuous at almost every Brownian path. - `ProbabilityTheory.IsBrownianReal.ae_continuousAt_shiftAtFirstNonnegativeWindowStartUpTo`: the same assertion for $\Phi_s$ at every fixed finite horizon $s$.

Source header “Brownian continuity of centered first-window paths”; Public declarations: The public theorems in this file are: - `ProbabilityTheory.IsBrownianReal.ae_continuousAt_centeredFirstWindowShift`: $f\mapsto(t\mapsto f(T(f)+t)-f(T(f)))$ is continuous at almost every Brownian path. - `ProbabilityTheory.IsBrownianReal.ae_continuousAt_centeredFirstWindowShiftUpTo`: the same assertion for $T^s$ at each finite $s$.

Source header “Brownian continuity of finite-horizon centered first-window paths”; Public declarations: The public theorem in this file is: - `ProbabilityTheory.IsBrownianReal.ae_continuousAt_centeredFirstWindowShiftFiniteHorizon`: for every finite $s$, the centered map $C([0,s],\mathbb R)\to C([0,1],\mathbb R)$ is continuous $P^s$-almost everywhere. This is the centered counterpart of the continuity step in Erwin Bolthausen, *On a Functional Central Limit Theorem for Random Walks Conditioned to Stay Positive*, Lemma 2.5 and Theorem 3.2, Ann. Probab. 4(3) (1976), 480--485, DOI 10.1214/aop/1176996098.

Source header “Removing a finite cutoff from Brownian first-window shifts”; Public declarations: The public theorem in this file is: - `ProbabilityTheory.IsBrownianReal.tendstoInDistribution_centeredFirstWindowShiftUpTo`: the laws of the centered Brownian paths shifted at $T^{n+1}$, restricted to $[0,1]$, converge to the law of the path shifted at $T$. This is the Brownian cutoff removal in equations (3.6)--(3.8) of Erwin Bolthausen, *On a Functional Central Limit Theorem for Random Walks Conditioned to Stay Positive*, Theorem 3.2, Ann. Probab. 4(3) (1976), 480--485, DOI 10.1214/aop/1176996098. Almost surely $T<\infty$, and every sufficiently large cutoff gives the same shifted path.

Source header “Finite-horizon Brownian first-window law”; Public declarations: The public theorem in this file is: - `ProbabilityTheory.IsBrownianReal.ae_continuousAt_firstWindowShiftFiniteHorizon`: for every finite $s$, the map $\Phi_s:C([0,s],\mathbb R)\to C([0,1],\mathbb R)$ is continuous $P^s$-almost everywhere, where $P^s=P\circ\Pi_s^{-1}$ is the Brownian path law projected to $[0,s]$. This is the path-space and measure-theoretic formulation of Erwin Bolthausen, *On a Functional Central Limit Theorem for Random Walks Conditioned to Stay Positive*, Lemma 2.5, Ann. Probab. 4(3) (1976), 480--485, DOI 10.1214/aop/1176996098.

Source header “Brownian continuity of finite-horizon first-window times”; Public declarations: The public theorem in this file is: - `ProbabilityTheory.IsBrownianReal.ae_continuousAt_firstWindowTimeFiniteHorizon`: for every finite $s$, the first eligible-window time on $C([0,s],\mathbb R)$ is continuous almost everywhere under the projected Brownian path law $P^s$. This is the finite-path form of Erwin Bolthausen, *On a Functional Central Limit Theorem for Random Walks Conditioned to Stay Positive*, Lemma 2.4, Ann. Probab. 4(3) (1976), 480--485, DOI 10.1214/aop/1176996098.

Chaumont--Doney, *Invariance principles for local times at the maximum of random walks and Lévy processes*, Theorem 6 (DOI 10.1214/09-AOP512), provides a later treatment of the meander limit.

Source header “Finite-variance survival at a diffusive horizon”; Internal proof declarations: - `ProbabilityTheory.RandomWalk.FunctionalLimit.Conditioned.exists_eventually_diffusiveSurvivalProbability_ge_inverse_square_of_centeredSecondMoment`: for centered increments of variance $\sigma^2>0$ and $N_n=\lfloor\Delta_n^2\rfloor-m$, there is $C>0$ such that $\mathbb P(C_{N_n})\ge C\Delta_n^{-2}$ eventually. The proof combines the cyclic rotation inequality of Bauer--Godrèche--Luck, *Statistics of persistent events in the binomial random walk: Will the drunken sailor hit the sober man?*, Appendix A, immediately after (A.3) (arXiv:cond-mat/9905252), with the Gaussian endpoint-sign limit.

Source header “Positive probabilities for conditioned transition corridors”; Internal proof declarations: - `ProbabilityTheory.RandomWalk.FunctionalLimit.Conditioned.exists_eventually_normalizedTransitionCorridorProbability_ge`: for $D_{\sigma,s}=\{f:\forall t\in[0,1],\ 0\le f(t)\le 5s/(6\sigma),\ f(1)\in[5s/(12\sigma),11s/(24\sigma)]\}$, if $Q_n\circ X_n^{-1}\Rightarrow\mathsf m$, the support of $\mathsf m$ contains $t\mapsto7t/(16\sigma)$, $X_n\ge0$ almost surely, and $s_n\to1$, then some $q>0$ satisfies $Q_n(X_n\in D_{\sigma,s_n})\ge q$ eventually. - `ProbabilityTheory.RandomWalk.FunctionalLimit.Conditioned.exists_eventually_interpolatedTransitionConditionalProbability_ge`: for the laws $Q_{n+1}$ of the increments conditioned on $S_j\ge0$ for $1\le j\le n+1$, the polygonal path limit with support at $t\mapsto7t/(16\sigma)$ and $\Delta_n/\sqrt{n+1}\to1$ imply $Q_{n+1}(D_{n+1,\Delta_n})\ge q$ eventually for some $q>0$.

Source header “Transition estimate from the centered first-window limit”; Internal proof declarations: - `ProbabilityTheory.RandomWalk.FunctionalLimit.Conditioned.exists_eventually_transitionConditionalProbability_ge_of_firstWindowSupport`: for centered unit-variance increments, if the Brownian first-window path law has $t\mapsto7t/16$ in its support and $\Delta_n/\sqrt{n+1}\to1$, then some $q>0$ satisfies $\mathbb P(D_{n+1,\Delta_n}\mid C_{n+1})\ge q$ eventually. The conditional path convergence is proved from the centered first-window construction of Erwin Bolthausen, *On a Functional Central Limit Theorem for Random Walks Conditioned to Stay Positive*, Ann. Probab. 4(3) (1976), 480--485, DOI 10.1214/aop/1176996098, Theorem 3.2. The support point is the remaining Brownian-meander identification used in Wang Yiyang, *Asymptotic Speed of the N-Branching Random Walk with Infinite Offspring* (master's thesis, Fudan University, 2026), Chapter 3, Lemma 3.5, and Appendix A.2, Lemma A.7.

Source header “Conditional transition probability from Brownian meander”; Internal proof declarations: - `ProbabilityTheory.RandomWalk.FunctionalLimit.Conditioned.exists_eventually_transitionConditionalProbability_ge_of_unitVariance`: if $S$ is a centered unit-variance walk and $\Delta_n/\sqrt{n+1}\to1$, then for some $q>0$, $\mathbb P(D_{n+1,\Delta_n}\mid S_1,\ldots,S_{n+1}\ge0)\ge q$ eventually. - `ProbabilityTheory.RandomWalk.FunctionalLimit.Conditioned.exists_eventually_transitionConditionalProbability_ge_of_centeredSecondMoment`: the same conclusion for variance $\sigma^2>0$, with paths normalized by $\sigma\sqrt n$.

Source header “Brownian corridor bounds for Donsker limits”; Public declarations: - `ProbabilityTheory.RandomWalk.brownian_skorokhodCorridor_le_liminf_strictTube`: for centered unit-variance increments and $0<a<1$, Brownian path-law mass of $\{f:-a<f(t)<1-a\ (0\le t\le1)\}$ is at most $\liminf_n\mathbb P(-a\sqrt n<S_j<(1-a)\sqrt n\ (1\le j\le n)$. - `ProbabilityTheory.RandomWalk.brownian_centeredSkorokhodCorridor_le_liminf_strictTube`: for each $w>0$, Brownian path-law mass of $\{f:|f(t)|<w/2\ (0\le t\le1)\}$ is at most the liminf of the matching strict-tube probabilities at width $w\sqrt n$.

Source header “Brownian corridor bounds with an endpoint constraint”; Public declarations: - `ProbabilityTheory.RandomWalk.brownian_centeredSkorokhodCorridorEndsIn_le_liminf_strictTubeEndsIn`: for centered unit-variance increments and $w>0$, Brownian path-law mass of $\{f:|f(t)|<w/2\ (0\le t\le1),\ f(1)\in(a,b)\}$ is at most $\liminf_n\mathbb P(|S_j|<w\sqrt n/2\ (1\le j\le n),\ S_n/\sqrt n\in(a,b))$. - `ProbabilityTheory.RandomWalk.limsup_centeredWeakTube_le_brownian_closedCorridor`: for centered unit-variance increments and $w\ge0$, the limsup probability of the weak centered tube is at most Brownian path-law mass of $\{f:|f(t)|\le w/2\ (0\le t\le1)\}$.

Source header “Finite-dimensional limits for Donsker's theorem”; Public declarations: - `ProbabilityTheory.RandomWalk.tendstoInDistribution_proportionalPartialSum`: $S_{\lfloor tn\rfloor}/\sqrt n\Rightarrow\sqrt tZ$ for $t>0$. - `ProbabilityTheory.RandomWalk.tendstoInDistribution_proportionalBlockSum`: a shifted block of length $\lfloor tn\rfloor$, divided by $\sqrt n$, converges to $N(0,t)$.

Source header “Random-walk limits on Brownian uniform grids”; Public declarations: - `ProbabilityTheory.RandomWalk.tendstoInDistribution_proportionalBlockEndpoints_brownian`: for centered increments with \(\mathbb E X_1^2=1\), the normalized endpoints \((S_{j\lfloor rn\rfloor}/\sqrt n)_{j=0}^m\) converge jointly in distribution to \((B_{jr})_{j=0}^m\) for each \(r>0\) and finite block count \(m\).

Source header “Uniform-grid limits for polygonal random-walk paths”; Public declarations: - `ProbabilityTheory.RandomWalk.tendstoInDistribution_normalizedLinearPath_uniformGrid_brownian`: for centered increments with \(\mathbb E X_1^2=1\), the normalized polygonal path values on the fixed grid \((j/m)_{j=0}^m\) converge jointly in distribution to \((B_{j/m})_{j=0}^m\).

Source header “Rational finite-dimensional Donsker limits”; Public declarations: - `ProbabilityTheory.RandomWalk.tendstoInDistribution_normalizedLinearPath_rationalFinite_brownian`: for \(n\ge1\), let \(w_{n,k}(t)=\min\{1,\max\{0,nt-k\}\}\) and \[ X_n(t)=\frac{1}{\sqrt n}\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}w_{n,k}(t)\xi_k. \] For centered i.i.d. increments with \(\mathbb E[\xi_0^2]=1\) and every finite \(I\subseteq\mathbb Q\cap[0,1]\), \[ (X_n(t))_{t\in I}\ \Rightarrow\ (B_t)_{t\in I}. \] - `ProbabilityTheory.RandomWalk.tendstoInDistribution_normalizedLinearPath_rationalFinite_continuousPath`: gives the same convergence, with the limit vector obtained by evaluating the continuous Brownian path at the times in \(I\).

Source header “Continuous-path Donsker theorem”; Public declarations: - `ProbabilityTheory.RandomWalk.tendstoInDistribution_normalizedLinearContinuousPath_brownian`: if $\int x\,d\nu=0$, $\int x^2\,d\nu=1$, and $B$ is a measurable, continuous pre-Brownian process, the normalized polygonal paths converge in law in $C([0,1],\mathbb R)$ to $B$. This is Donsker's invariance principle, stated as Theorem 4.20 in I. Karatzas and S. E. Shreve, *Brownian Motion and Stochastic Calculus*, 2nd ed., Graduate Texts in Mathematics 113, Springer (1991), DOI 10.1007/978-1-4612-0949-2.

Source header “Continuous-path corridor adapters”; Public declarations: - `ProbabilityTheory.RandomWalk.measure_openCorridor_le_liminf_strictTube_of_functionalLimit`: given a functional limit and $0<a<1$, the limiting mass of paths with range in $(-a,1-a)$ is at most the liminf of the corresponding `InOpenHorizontalTube` probabilities for the normalized walks. - `ProbabilityTheory.RandomWalk.limsup_weakTube_le_measure_closedCorridor_of_functionalLimit`: given a functional limit and $0\le a\le1$, the limsup of the `InHorizontalTube` probabilities is at most the limiting mass of paths with range in $[-a,1-a]$.

Source header “Finite-horizon polygonal random-walk paths”; Public declarations: - `ProbabilityTheory.RandomWalk.tendstoInDistribution_normalizedLinearContinuousPath_finiteHorizon_scaledBrownian`: for centered, unit-second-moment increments and every positive integer $m$, the path on $[0,m]$ converges to $t\mapsto\sqrt m B(t/m)$. - `ProbabilityTheory.RandomWalk.tendstoInDistribution_normalizedLinearContinuousPath_finiteHorizon_brownian`: when $B$ is Brownian, the same finite-horizon limit has the projected law $P^m$.

Source header “Skorokhod-space Donsker theorem”; Public declarations: - `ProbabilityTheory.RandomWalk.tendstoInDistribution_normalizedStepCadlagPath_brownian`: if $\int x\,d\nu=0$, $\int x^2\,d\nu=1$, and $B$ is a measurable, continuous pre-Brownian process, the normalized step paths converge in Skorokhod $J_1$ to the image of $B$. This is the step-path form of Theorem 4.20 in I. Karatzas and S. E. Shreve, *Brownian Motion and Stochastic Calculus*, 2nd ed., Graduate Texts in Mathematics 113, Springer (1991), DOI 10.1007/978-1-4612-0949-2.

Source header “Parameters for the diffusive oscillation estimate”; Internal proof declarations: - `ProbabilityTheory.RandomWalk.exists_proportionalBlockParameters` (internal): for positive $\epsilon$ and $\eta$, choose $b\in\mathbb N$ and $q,c,\delta>0$ such that $1<bq$, $9\delta=\epsilon$, and $b(8qc^2+3q^2)/\delta^4<\eta$. This theorem is used only to finish the fourth-moment oscillation estimate in `Donsker.Tightness.Path`.

Source header “Global bounds for normalized polygonal paths”; Public declarations: - `ProbabilityTheory.RandomWalk.eventually_normalizedLinearPathLaw_oscillation`: for every $\epsilon>0$ and $\eta>0$, some $\delta>0$ satisfies $\mathbb P(\omega_\delta(X_n)>\epsilon)<\eta$ eventually, where $X_n$ is the diffusively normalized polygonal path. - `ProbabilityTheory.RandomWalk.normalizedLinearPathLaw_compl_uniformBound_le`: for $R>0$ and $n>0$, $\mathbb P(\sup_{0\le t\le1}|X_n(t)|>R)\le R^{-2}$.

Source header “Random walks killed outside a measurable set”; Public declarations: For a measurable allowed set $A\subseteq E$, `killedIncrementKernel` is the additive transition kernel restricted to $A$, and `killedIncrementKernelOn` uses $A$ itself as the state space. The public constructions and theorems are: - `killedIncrementKernel`, `killedIncrementKernelOn`: the ambient and restricted-state one-step kernels killed on exit from $A$. - `killedStep`: the option-valued step $x,z\mapsto \operatorname{some}(x+z)$ when $x+z\in A$, and `none` otherwise.

Source header “Comparison of killed-walk survival masses”; Public declarations: For a real random walk, the public theorems are: - `remainingMass_killedIncrementKernel_Icc_mono_of_abs_sub_le`: if $|x-y|\le\delta$, survival for $n$ steps from $y$ in the shrunken interval $[a+\delta,b-\delta]$ is bounded above by survival from $x$ in $[a,b]$. - `le_remainingMass_killedIncrementKernel_Icc_of_finset`: a finite $\delta$-net of $[a,b]$ transfers a common shrunken-interval lower bound $p$ to every starting point in $[a,b]$.

Source header “Equal-block representation of killed-walk survival”; Public declarations: For $m,\ell\ge1$, the public theorems identify the killed kernel's remaining mass through $m\ell$ steps with the probability that every point in every length-$\ell$ block lies in the closed interval: - `killedIncrementKernelOn_Icc_remainingMass_mul_eq_blockCorridors`: the restricted-state identity for an initial point in $[a,b]$. - `killedIncrementKernel_Icc_remainingMass_mul_eq_blockCorridors`: the ambient-state identity, assuming the initial point lies in $[a,b]$.

Source header “Killed block kernels returning to an interior set”; Public declarations: Let $\kappa_A$ be the additive kernel killed outside a measurable set $A$, and let $R$ be any measurable return set. `returnKernel` runs $\ell$ steps of $\kappa_A$ and retains endpoints in $R$. The public declarations are: - `returnKernel`: the resulting transition kernel on the state space $R$. - `returnKernel_apply_univ`: $\rho_\ell(x,R)=(\kappa_A^\ell)(x,R)$ for $x\in R$.

Source header “Terminal bridges after killed return blocks”; Public declarations: For measurable $\mathrm{core},\mathrm{target}\subseteq\mathrm{allowed}$, if each return block has mass at least $p$ from every core point and the final killed bridge has mass at least $q$, then the IID probability of staying in `allowed` for the total scheduled time and ending in `target` is at least $p^m q$, where $m$ is the number of return blocks. - `iidSequenceLaw_staysIn_endsIn_ge_of_returnSequenceExit`: this lower bound for an arbitrary finite list of return-block lengths followed by one exit bridge.

Source header “Comparison of killed return kernels”; Public declarations: For a real random walk, the public theorems transfer return-block mass from shrunken intervals to a finite net and then to every starting point: - `returnKernel_Icc_apply_univ_mono_of_abs_sub_le`: if $|x-y|\le\delta$, the return-block mass from $y$ in the shrunken outer and return intervals is at most the mass from $x$ in the full intervals. - `le_returnKernel_Icc_apply_univ_of_finset`: a finite $\delta$-net of the return interval transfers a common lower bound to every starting point.

Source header “Entrance lower bounds for killed random walks”; Public declarations: The public theorems give lower bounds for a killed transition to a target: - `pow_measure_le_killedIncrementKernel_pow_apply_of_forall_mem`: if every length-$n$ increment sequence in a measurable increment set keeps the walk in `allowed` and ends in `target`, then $\nu(\mathrm{incrementSet})^n\le (\kappa_{\mathrm{allowed}}^n)(x, \mathrm{target})$. - `pow_measure_Ioo_le_killedIncrementKernel_pow_apply`: if the deterministic intervals $[x+k\ell,x+ku]$ stay in `allowed` for $k\le n$ and the final one lies in `target`, then $\nu((\ell,u))^n\le (\kappa_{\mathrm{allowed}}^n)(x,\mathrm{target})$.

Source header “Endpoint laws of killed random walks”; Public declarations: For a probability measure $\nu$, measurable allowed set $A$, and initial point $x$, the public declarations are: - `killedEndpointLaw`: the image law of the endpoint of the IID walk restricted to histories that stay in $A$ for $n$ steps. - `killedEndpointLaw_eq_killedIncrementKernel_pow_apply`: this endpoint law is the transition measure $(\kappa_A^n)(x,\cdot)$.

Source header “Horizontal tubes and killed return kernels”; Public declarations: For $n\ge1$, the public theorems bound strict horizontal-tube probabilities by the mass of an appropriate killed return kernel: - `strictTubeProbability_le_returnKernel_centeredIcc`: a tube of width $d$ centered at $0$ is bounded by the kernel killed outside a wider interval and returned to the inner interval. - `strictTubeProbability_le_returnKernel_centeredIcc_from`: the same bound for a tube translated to a starting point inside the initial interval, provided both outer and return widths contain the translated tube.

Source header “Equal-block path interpretation of interval return kernels”; Public declarations: For positive block count and block length, the public theorem `returnKernel_Icc_apply_univ_mul_eq_blockCorridors_endsIn` identifies a return-kernel mass after `blocks * length` steps with the IID probability that all points in every block stay in the outer interval and the final endpoint lies in the return interval.

Source header “Uniform iteration bounds for killed return kernels”; Public declarations: These estimates turn uniform one-block return mass into lower bounds for iterated return kernels and for the ambient killed walk. Along the filter, the scale need only be positive at indices where the one-block estimate is used. The results do not depend on a Mogulskii normalization or a moment assumption. For scale $s_i>0$, let $R_i$ be the return kernel formed from the walk killed outside $[s_i a,s_i b]$, with return interval $[s_i c,s_i d]$ and block length $\ell_i$. If every row of $R_i$ has mass at least $p$, then \[ p^k\leq \operatorname{remainingMass}(R_i,k,s_i x), \qquad p^{\lfloor N/\ell_i\rfloor+1} \leq \operatorname{remainingMass}(K_i,N,s_i x), \] where $K_i$ is the killed-walk kernel and $x\in[c,d]$. Source header “Blocking horizontal-tube probabilities”; Public declarations: For $0\le a\le1$, width $D\ge0$, and horizon $n$, the public theorems are: - `remainingMass_killedIncrementKernel_scaled_Icc_eq_horizontalTubeProbability`: the ambient killed-kernel survival mass from $0$ in $[-aD,(1-a)D]$ equals `horizontalTubeProbability`. - `remainingMass_killedIncrementKernelOn_Icc_eq_horizontalTubeProbability`: the same identity for the restricted-state interval kernel.

Source header “Uniform killed-kernel bounds from finite liminf estimates”; Public declarations: The public theorems transfer real-interval bounds to uniform bounds on the restricted-state kernel: - `eventually_forall_le_remainingMass_killedIncrementKernelOn_Icc_of_normalized`: an eventual normalized lower bound on every $x\in[a,b]$ gives the same bound for every state in the scaled interval. - `eventually_pow_succ_div_le_remainingMass_killedIncrementKernelOn_Icc`: if the normalized one-block mass is eventually at least $p$, then the remaining mass over duration $N_i$ is eventually at least $p^{\lfloor N_i/m_i\rfloor+1}$ for every state in the scaled interval.

Source header “Increment paths of random walks”; Public declarations: - `positionProcess x n ξ` is the position \(X_n(ξ)=x+\sum_{j<n}ξ_j\). `positionProcess_zero` and `positionProcess_succ` state (X_0=x) and (X_{n+1}=X_n+ξ_n). - `displacement_measurable`, `measurable_natAdd`, `positionProcess_measurable`, and `positionProcess_path_measurable` give measurability of accumulated displacements, deterministic shifts, and the position process under the stated measurable-addition assumptions.

Source header “Measurable increment blocks”; Public declarations: `blockSum_measurable` states that for a measurable additive monoid $E$, the finite block sum $x\mapsto\sum_{j<\ell}x_{a+j}$ is measurable on the canonical increment-path space.

Source header “Finite increment-block corridor predicates”; Public declarations: * `InOpenPartialSumCorridor lower upper block` is `∀ k : Fin (length + 1), lower < Fin.partialSum block k ∧ Fin.partialSum block k < upper`. * `inOpenPartialSumCorridor_iff_succ` identifies this predicate with `∀ k : Fin length, lower < Fin.partialSum block k.succ ∧ Fin.partialSum block k.succ < upper` when `lower < 0 < upper`.

Source header “Probability bounds for block corridors”; Public declarations: * `measure_startMargin_le_blockCorridor_add_largeDeviation` states that the `incrementLaw {ω | lower + radius ≤ AdditivePath.displacement start ω ∧ AdditivePath.displacement start ω ≤ upper - radius}` is at most `incrementLaw {ω | ∀ k ≤ length, AdditivePath.displacement (start + k) ω ∈ Set.Icc lower upper}` plus `incrementLaw {ω | ∃ k ∈ Finset.range (length + 1), radius ≤ |AdditivePath.blockSum start (k + 1) ω|}`.

Source header “Finite-block corridor core returns”; Public declarations: - `InOpenPartialSumCoreReturn a b c₀ r₀ c₁ r₁ z` means \[ a+r_0-c_0 < S_k(z) < b-r_0-c_0\quad(0\le k\le \ell), \qquad c_1-c_0-\frac{r_1-r_0}{2}<S_\ell(z)<c_1-c_0+\frac{r_1-r_0}{2}. \] - `measurableSet_inOpenPartialSumCoreReturn` proves measurability in the finite product sigma algebra.

Source header “Finite bridge comparisons for IID random walks”; Public declarations: * `FiniteBridgeGeometry ι F prefixLength bridgeLength U T` records measurable prefix and bridge cells, a finite cover of `U`, and the implication that joining each prefix cell to its bridge cell gives an event contained in `T`. * `eventually_uniform_bridge_lower_bound_of_open_path_limit` gives one eventual positive lower bound for the bridge probabilities of a finite family from open-set convergence in distribution.

Source header “Geometry of finite block corridors”; Public declarations: Let $D(t)=\operatorname{displacement}(t)$ and $B(s,k)=\operatorname{blockSum}(s,k)$. If $|B(s,k)|\le r$ for every $k\le n$, then `abs_partialSum_add_sub_partialSum_add_le_two_mul` gives $|D(s+\ell)-D(s+k)|\le2r$ for $k,\ell\le n$, and `abs_partialSum_nextBlock_add_sub_partialSum_add_le_three_mul` gives the corresponding $3r$ bound for positions in consecutive blocks. `displacement_mem_Icc_of_start_mem_shrunken` and `displacement_mem_Ioo_of_start_mem_shrunken` show that a block start in the interval contracted by $r$, together with a block deviation bounded by $r$, keeps all positions in the original closed or open interval. Finally, `startMargin_subset_blockCorridor_union_largeDeviation` states the endpoint-margin dichotomy: an increment path starting in the shrunken corridor either remains in the corridor throughout the block or has a relative block displacement at least as large as the prescribed radius.

Source header “Measurability of finite-block corridor events”; Public declarations: * `measurableSet_inOpenPartialSumCorridor` proves measurability of the event that every finite partial sum lies in an open interval. * `measurableSet_inOpenPartialSumCorridorEndsIn` adds an open terminal window for the final partial sum and proves measurability of the resulting event.

Source header “Finite-variance tilted-tube endpoint bounds”; Public declarations: The public theorem in this file is: - `ProbabilityTheory.RandomWalk.SmallDeviation.DriftedTube.exists_uniform_driftedTube_endpoint_bounds`: if the increment law has mean zero and variance $\sigma^2>0$, $v>0$, $c\ge0$, $\varepsilon>0$, and $d'>\pi^2\sigma^2/2$, one width threshold gives $e^{-d'L/\Delta^2}\le\mathbb P(A^-_{L,\Delta})$ and $e^{-d'L/\Delta^2}\le\mathbb P(A^+_{L,\Delta})$ for every admissible initial boundary and horizon $L\ge\lfloor\Delta^{2+\varepsilon}\rfloor$. For increments $\xi=(\xi_i)_{i\ge0}$, write $Y_j=\sum_{i=0}^{j-1}\xi_i$ and $R_j=r+\mu j/\Delta^2$. These events are $A^-_{L,\Delta}=\{R_j\le Y_j\le R_j+\Delta\ (1\le j\le L),\; Y_L\in[R_L,R_L+v\Delta]\}$ and $A^+_{L,\Delta}=\{R_j\le Y_j\le R_j+\Delta\ (1\le j\le L),\; Y_L\in[R_L+(1-v)\Delta,R_L+\Delta]\}$. This is Wang Yiyang, *Asymptotic Speed of the N-Branching Random Walk with Infinite Offspring*, Chapter 3, Lemma 3.5. Its parameter selection follows that proof: first choose an intermediate exponential rate, then a finite bin count, strict window margins, and an intermediate power block length. Mogul'skii, “Small deviations in the sample function space,” *Teoriya Veroyatnostei i ee Primeneniya* 19(4) (1974), 755--765; English translation, “Small Deviations in a Space of Trajectories,” *Theory of Probability and Its Applications* 19(4) (1975), 726--736, DOI 10.1137/1119081.

Source header “Stable clock increments”; Public declarations: - HasStableClockIncrements requires a strictly $\alpha$-stable reference law, a monotone clock $c$ with $c(\bot)=0$, zero start, independent increments, and increment law $X_t-X_s\sim (x\mapsto(c(t)-c(s))^{1/\alpha}x)_\#\mu$. - Monotone time changes, translated time changes, positive space scalings, and the matching stable time-space rescaling preserve this specification.

Source header “Brownian motion as a stable Lévy process”; Public declarations: - `IsPreBrownianReal.hasStableClockIncrements`: Brownian increments satisfy $B_t-B_s\sim N(0,t-s)$, hence the exponent-two stable clock law. - `IsBrownianReal.isStableLevyProcess`: an almost-surely continuous process with $B_t-B_s\sim N(0,t-s)$ is a Gaussian stable Lévy process.

`IsBrownianReal.isStableClockProcessLaw_cadlagunitIntervalProcessPathLaw` identifies Mathlib Brownian motion's càdlàg path law with the canonical stable unit-interval path law. Its public type uses `IsBrownianReal.isStableLevyProcess` and its public import exposes that stable-process adapter.

Source header “Law invariance of stable corridor events”; Public declarations: - If two stable Lévy processes have the same index and increment law, their rational range-tube probabilities agree at every width: $P_X(\mathrm{tube}(a))=P_Y(\mathrm{tube}(a))$. The rational event-law transfer itself is stated in the generic corridor module. This result supplies the rational-time process law from the stable increment specification.

Source header “Finite-dimensional laws of stable-increment processes”; Public declarations: - `HasStableClockIncrements.finiteDimensional_identDistrib` states that matching stable increment specifications imply \(\operatorname{Law}((X_{t_j})_{j=1}^n)= \operatorname{Law}((Y_{t_j})_{j=1}^n)\) on each finite monotone grid. - `HasStableClockIncrements.finiteRestriction_identDistrib` gives the same equality for \((X_t)_{t\in I}\) and \((Y_t)_{t\in I}\) on every finite \(I\) in a linearly ordered time type.

Source header “Endpoint law of the stable jump-sum model”; Public declarations: * `IsStrictlyAlphaStable.law_unitTime_split_poissonRandomMeasures` identifies the sum of the small- and large-jump Poisson integrals with `μ`. * `IsStrictlyAlphaStable.law_poissonEntrancePath_cutoff_top` identifies the cutoff entrance-path endpoint with `μ`.
Finite disjoint windows have product stable law; cutoff Poisson model uses each window mass raised to 1/α as its spatial scale.
The cutoff entrance-path increment on [s,t] has stable law scaled by Lebesgue mass |(s,t]|^(1/α); finite-window vector law is a separate interface.
Canonical Poisson entrance path has independent increments and the stable clock-increment specification; formulas now match both public theorem types.

Source header “Stable Lévy processes”; Public declarations: - `ProbabilityTheory.IsStableLevyProcess α μ X P` is the identity-clock specialization of `IsStableClockProcess` on nonnegative real time. - `ProbabilityTheory.IsStableLevyProcess.spatialScale` preserves the process class under `X ↦ c X` and `μ ↦ μ.map (c ·)` for `c > 0`.

Source header “Stable process laws on càdlàg path space”; Public declarations: - `IsStableClockProcessLaw` specifies a path law $P$ whose coordinate process starts at zero, has independent increments, and satisfies $X_t-X_s\sim\mu_{c(t)-c(s)}$ for the given clock $c$. - Its projections expose strict stability, the almost-sure zero start, independent increments, increment laws, and the induced process instance. `law_of_pathMap_ae` transfers this interface across almost-surely equal path maps.

Source header “Concatenating independent unit-time stable path blocks”; Public declarations: The public construction takes the countable product of a unit-interval path law and concatenates its independent blocks on $[0,\infty)$. It proves the result is almost surely càdlàg, identifies each unit block with the input law, and gives the product law of increments over integer intervals. The final construction theorem recovers a full stable-clock path law from consistent unit-interval position-grid laws; grid-factorization details remain private.

Source header “Full-time stable processes from unit-time path laws”; Public declarations: The public theorems show that concatenated i.i.d. unit-interval stable path blocks form a full stable Lévy process: increments on disjoint time intervals are independent, each increment has its clock-scaled stable law, and every finite increment vector has the corresponding product law. The final theorem identifies the canonical unit-interval path-law restriction with the given block law. Measurability of individual block coordinates remains private.

Source header “Gaussian stable path laws near linear paths”; Public declarations: For a Gaussian stable path law and every continuous linear path $\ell$ and radius $\epsilon>0$, the public theorems give positive mass to the uniform path ball $\{f:\|f-\ell\|_\infty<\epsilon\}$. The statements cover an actual stable Lévy process, its path law, and an abstract stable-clock path law. The Brownian bridge and endpoint independence calculations are private.

Source header “Stable position laws on monotone time grids”; Public declarations: - `ProbabilityTheory.stableGridPositionLaws_of_strictGridPositionLaws`: strict-grid stable increment laws imply both the almost-sure zero-start property and the position-vector law on every monotone grid. For each monotone `t` with `t 0 = ⊥`, `P.map (denseEvaluation t) = (stableTimeLawProductProbability α t).map Fin.partialSum`.

`IsStableLevyProcess.unitIntervalPathLaw` specializes the general `IsLevyProcess.unitIntervalPathLaw` at horizon $1$; `isStableClockProcessLaw_unitIntervalPathLaw` proves the stable clock-law characterization. The duplicated canonical path-law construction was removed.
Internal coordinate and product-measure derivations used only by the monotone-grid theorem; changed to package-local declarations and consumed with import all. Focused parent build passed.

Source header “Stable clock processes”; Public declarations: - `ProbabilityTheory.IsStableClockProcess α μ clock X P` specifies stable clock increments and almost-sure càdlàg paths: `HasStableClockIncrements α μ clock X P ∧ ∀ᵐ ω ∂P, IsCadlag (fun t => X t ω)`. - `ProbabilityTheory.IsStableClockProcess.increments` projects the stable clock-increment specification.

Source header “Deterministic shifts of stable Lévy processes”; Public declarations: - `ProbabilityTheory.IsStableLevyProcess.shift` states that for every deterministic $s\geq 0$, the recentered process $Y_t=X_{s+t}-X_s$ remains a stable Lévy process with the same stable law. Its generic Lévy-process path properties follow from `ProbabilityTheory.IsLevyProcess.shift`.

Source header “Billingsley convergence from aligned path limits”; Internal proof declarations: `Skorokhod.Completion.Lemmas.summablyAligned_subsequence_tendsto_billingsley` states that if the successive Billingsley costs are bounded by a summable sequence and the cumulative time-change alignment converges uniformly to a càdlàg path $g$, then there is a Billingsley path $f$ such that \[ f_{k(n)} \longrightarrow f \quad\text{in Billingsley's logarithmic metric}. \] The uniformly convergent aligned paths give a Billingsley limit after composing with the inverse of the limiting cumulative clock. Tail clocks control the logarithmic part of the distance. This is the limit-identification part of Theorem 14.2 in Patrick Billingsley, *Convergence of Probability Measures*, 1st ed., Wiley, 1968, Chapter 3, §14, equations (A4.30)–(A4.31), pp. 115–116 ([text](https://ru.djvu.online/file/vaaIHv9IWlVeK)). Review context: “Skorokhod extended-distance audit (2026-10-29)” in MODULE_DIRECTORY_AUDIT.md.

Source header “Cauchy subsequence extraction for logarithmic Skorokhod completeness”; Internal proof declarations: `Skorokhod.Completion.Lemmas.cauchySeq_subsequence_has_summableLogAlignment` states that, for a Cauchy sequence $(f_n)$ in Billingsley's path metric over a complete metric state space, there exist a strictly increasing index map $k$, a summable error sequence $(\varepsilon_n)$, time changes $(\lambda_n)$, and a càdlàg path $g$ such that \[ \sum_n \varepsilon_n < \infty,\qquad \operatorname{billingsleyCost} (f_{k(n+1)}^{\mathrm{cad}},f_{k(n)}^{\mathrm{cad}},\lambda_n) <\varepsilon_n,\qquad \operatorname{alignedPath} \bigl((f_{k(m)}^{\mathrm{cad}})_{m\ge0},(\lambda_m)_{m\ge0},n\bigr) \longrightarrow g \quad\text{uniformly in }n. \] Here $f_j^{\mathrm{cad}}$ is the underlying càdlàg path of the Billingsley path $f_j$, and `alignedPath` composes it with the cumulative time changes. A Cauchy sequence in Billingsley's metric has a subsequence with summably small consecutive distances. Choosing time changes that witness these distances produces a uniformly convergent aligned subsequence. This is the extraction and clock-selection part of Theorem 14.2 in Patrick Billingsley, *Convergence of Probability Measures*, 1st ed., Wiley, 1968, Chapter 3, §14, equations (A4.27)–(A4.29), p. 115 ([text](https://ru.djvu.online/file/vaaIHv9IWlVeK)). Review context: “Skorokhod extended-distance audit (2026-10-29)” in MODULE_DIRECTORY_AUDIT.md.
